title: Krishna
wiki_lead:
Krishna (; Sanskrit: कृष्ण, lit. 'Black', IAST: Kṛṣṇa Sanskrit: [ˈkr̩ʂɳɐ] )  also known as Govinda, Madhava, Gopala, and other names and titles is a major deity in Hinduism. He is worshipped as the eighth avatar of Vishnu and as the Supreme God in his own right. He is widely revered for his divine qualities of love, compassion, protection, and tenderness. Krishna's birthday is celebrated every year by Hindus on Krishna Janmashtami, according to the lunisolar Hindu calendar, which falls in late August or early September of the Gregorian calendar.
Krishna is often depicted in dark skin in accordance with meaning of his name, "black" or "dark". The anecdotes and narratives of Krishna's life are known as Krishna Lila. He is a central figure in the Mahabharata, the Bhagavata Purana, the Brahma Vaivarta Purana, and the Bhagavad Gita, and is mentioned in many Hindu philosophical, theological, and mythological texts. These texts describes him as a divine statesman, teacher, savior of dharma, charioteer, and sometimes a cowherd. They portray him in various perspectives: as a god-child, a prankster, a model lover, a divine hero, and the universal supreme being. His iconography reflects these legends and shows him in different stages of his life, such as an infant eating butter, a young boy playing a flute, a handsome youth with Radha or surrounded by female devotees, or a friendly charioteer giving counsel to Arjuna.
Krishna was born in Mathura to Devaki and Vasudeva, but was raised by Nanda and Yashoda in Gokul to escape his maternal uncle, the tyrant king Kamsa. His life, as given in texts, incorporates highly symbolic miraculous elements: he enchanted the gopis with his divine flute playing, performed the celestial Rasa Lila, and lifted Govardhan Hill to protect his community from devastating rains. He later defeated Kamsa and restored order in Mathura. He went on to establish the city of Dvaraka and played a central role in the Kurukshetra War, serving as Arjuna’s charioteer and delivering the philosophical teachings of the Bhagavad Gita.
The name and synonyms of Krishna have been traced to 1st millennium BCE literature and cults. In some sub-traditions within Hinduism, such as Krishnaism, Krishna is worshipped as the Supreme God and Svayam Bhagavan (God Himself) as he was master in all 64 forms of Art and 14 Vidya. These sub-traditions arose in the context of the medieval-era Bhakti movement. Krishna-related literature has inspired numerous performance arts such as Bharatanatyam, Kathakali, Kuchipudi, Odissi, and Manipuri dance. He is a pan-India god, but is particularly revered in some locations, such as Vrindavan in Uttar Pradesh, Dwarka and Junagadh in Gujarat, the Jagannatha aspect in Odisha, Mayapur in West Bengal, and other places. He is also worshipped in different regional forms across India.
Since the 1960s, the worship of Krishna has also spread to the Western world, largely due to the work of the Bhaktivedanta Swami and his organisation, ISKCON.

Names and epithets

The name "Krishna" originates from the Sanskrit word kṛṣṇa, which means "black", "dark" or "dark blue". The term is also associated with the Krishna Paksha, waning phase of the moon carrying its adjective meaning "darkening". In accordance with the meaning of the name, Krishna murtis are often depicted with black or blue skin.
As a name of Vishnu, Krishna it appears as the 57th name in the Vishnu Sahasranama.
Krishna is also known by various other names, epithets, and titles that reflecting his diverse associations and attributes. Among the most common names are:

Achyuta (Sanskrit: अच्युत): The infallible one; one who never falls from his divine nature
Ananta (Sanskrit: अनन्त): The endless or infinite one
Bāl Gopāl (Sanskrit: बाल गोपाल): The child Krishna; protector of cows
Bānke Bihārī (Sanskrit: बाँके बिहारी): The charming, graceful one who enjoys divine play
Chakrapāṇi (Sanskrit: चक्रपाणि): One who holds the Sudarshana Chakra (disc or wheel)

grok_lead: Krishna is a central deity in Hinduism, revered as the eighth and most significant avatar ( incarnation) of the god Vishnu, and in various traditions, such as Gaudiya Vaishnavism, worshipped as the Supreme God ( Svayam Bhagavan) in his own right. He embodies divine playfulness (lila), compassion, and wisdom. Celebrated as Bhaktavatsala (the lover of his devotees), he exemplifies humble service to his devotees through his role as Arjuna's charioteer (Parthasarathi) and his miraculous protection of Draupadi during her attempted disrobing in the Mahabharata, thereby demonstrating his mercy, love, and willingness to serve his bhaktas. He appears in ancient texts as a multifaceted figure who combines roles as a heroic warrior-prince, a mischievous child, a romantic lover, and a philosophical teacher. Krishna's mythology draws primarily from epic and Puranic literature, with his narratives evolving from the late Vedic period onward, gaining prominence in the first millennium CE. In the Sanskrit epic Mahabharata, composed between approximately 400 BCE and 400 CE (with the events and Krishna's life traditionally dated to c. 3200â3100 BCE based on ancient astronomical calculations and inscriptions such as those referenced by Aryabhata and the Aihole inscription), Krishna emerges as a key ally to the Pandava brothers during the Kurukshetra War, serving as Arjuna's charioteer and delivering the Bhagavad Gita, a 700-verse dialogue that outlines core Hindu philosophies including karma yoga (path of selfless action), bhakti yoga (path of devotion), and jnana yoga (path of knowledge). This discourse, set on the battlefield, emphasizes dharma (righteous duty) and the immortality of the soul, positioning Krishna as the ultimate guide to spiritual liberation ( moksha). The Bhagavad Gita remains one of the most influential texts in Hindu philosophy, translated and commented upon extensively since the medieval period. Krishna's early life and divine exploits are elaborated in the Bhagavata Purana (also known as Srimad Bhagavatam), a devotional text dated by scholars to between the 5th and 10th centuries CE, particularly in its tenth book, which describes his birth in Mathura to Devaki and Vasudeva amid persecution by his uncle Kamsa, and his subsequent upbringing in the pastoral village of Vrindavan (or Gokula). As a child, Krishna is portrayed as a butter-stealing prankster who slays demons like Putana and Aghasura, protecting the cowherd community (gopas and gopis), while his youthful phase highlights romantic and ecstatic devotion through the rasa lila, a cosmic dance with the gopis led by his beloved Radha, symbolizing the soul's union with the divine. These stories underscore themes of bhakti, portraying Krishna's leelas as metaphors for divine love transcending social norms. Worship of Krishna spans diverse sects and regions, with major pilgrimage sites including Mathura (his birthplace), Vrindavan (youthful abode), Dwarka (his kingdom), and Kurukshetra (battlefield site), where festivals like Janmashtami celebrate his birth and Holi his playful spirit. Iconography often depicts him as dark-skinned (the name Krishna derives from "black" or "dark"), playing the flute, adorned with peacock feathers, or in paired forms with Radha, influencing art, sculpture, and performing arts from medieval temple traditions to modern global movements like the International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON). Scholarly studies explore Krishna's historicity, with some evidence suggesting a possible tribal hero deified around the 1st millennium BCE, though his divine persona dominates religious narratives. His enduring appeal lies in bridging philosophy and devotion, making him a symbol of accessible divinity in Hindu thought and culture worldwide.
